nomenclature.en: Development of the Lens (Placode, Vesicle and Nuclei)

content.definition: The lens is a derivative of the surface ectoderm: by 27 days of gestation (embryo 4-4.5 mm) localized elongation of the surface cells produces the lens placode, which invaginates to form the lens vesicle at approximately 29 days; by about 33 days of gestation (8-10 mm stage) the separation is complete and the spherical lens vesicle, approximately 0.2 mm in diameter, comes to lie inside the eye. The posterior cells elongate to obliterate the vesicle cavity by 45 days of gestation (20 mm stage) and are preserved as the compact core of the lens, the embryonic nucleus; thereafter secondary lens fibres, laid down throughout life, encircle the primary fibres, and structurally the lens develops into three components — the capsule, the epithelium, and the lens cells or fibres (pp. 660-661).
content.location: The lens develops from the surface ectoderm overlying the optic vesicle: the placode and its underlying basal lamina are separated from the optic vesicle by a narrow space that contains a fine filamentous material (Silver and Wakely, 1974), thought to have a role in the gradual invagination of the placode. The vesicle sinks into the orifice of the optic cup, remaining attached to the surface ectoderm by the lens stalk until a zone of extreme attenuation and necrosis develops in the stalk and separation is complete at about 33 days; the basal surface of the vesicle cells remains outward and applied to the original basal lamina that envelops the vesicle completely and, with continued synthesis and secretion by the lens cells, this thickens to form the lens capsule (Tripathi and Tripathi, 1983; 1984) (p. 660). In the developed eye the lens lies behind the iris and pupil, suspended by the zonules from the ciliary body.
layers: Lens placode (27 days; embryo 4-4.5 mm) — localized ectodermal thickening produced by elongation of the surface cells; the placode and its underlying basal lamina are separated from the optic vesicle by a narrow space containing fine filamentous material (Silver and Wakely, 1974) (Fig 17.6) (p. 660).

Lens vesicle (about 29 days) — invagination of the placode forms the vesicle, its formation being marked on the surface of the embryo by a depression known as the lens pit or pore; within the vesicle the apices of the cuboidal cells are directed toward the central cavity, the basal surface outward to the enveloping basal lamina (Figs 17.66a,b; 17.67a) (p. 660).

Lens stalk and separation — the vesicle remains attached to the surface ectoderm by the lens stalk; a zone of extreme attenuation and necrosis develops in the stalk and, by about 33 days of gestation (8-10 mm stage), separation is complete and the spherical vesicle, approximately 0.2 mm in diameter, lies inside the eye (p. 660).

Embryonic nucleus and primary lens fibres — as the vesicle closes, the rate of DNA synthesis of the cells subjacent to the neural retina decreases and their content of cytoplasmic organelles reduces; they begin to synthesize crystallins and, beginning at about 5 weeks (embryo 12 mm), increase in length, extending towards the anterior surface so that the lumen is obliterated by 45 days of gestation (20 mm stage). The primary lens fibres attach firmly to the apical surface of the anterior lens epithelial cells through fascia adherens tight junctions; their nuclei migrate anteriorly and disintegrate. The posterior cells are preserved as the compact core of the lens — the embryonic nucleus — and the posterior aspect of the lens becomes devoid of epithelium (Tripathi and Tripathi, 1983) (pp. 660-661).

Lens bow and secondary fibres — the epithelial cells in the pre-equatorial region retain their mitotic and proliferative activity throughout life; the secondary lens fibres formed are displaced inwards toward the embryonic nucleus, elongating axially towards the two poles beneath the epithelium anteriorly and the capsule posteriorly, and their nuclei migrate progressively toward the anterior lens surface to give the distinctive lens bow. In a transient stage contralateral fibres from different equatorial quadrants are long enough to reach both poles; with successive internalization new fibres instead meet at radiating sutures — an erect Y anteriorly and an inverted Y posteriorly — first seen at about the 35 mm stage (approximately 8.5 weeks of gestation), persisting through the entire thickness of the fetal nucleus and throughout life as a hallmark of lens development; the sutures become more complex in the infantile and adult nucleus (Fig 17.67) (p. 661).

Changes in lens shape — the lens is initially elongated in the anteroposterior direction, becomes approximately spherical at the 18-24 mm stage and, with the appearance of secondary lens fibres at the 26 mm stage, wider in the equatorial diameter; it increases rapidly in mass and volume and expands in both sagittal and equatorial planes. At birth the lens is almost spheroidal, slightly wider in the equatorial plane (Bran and Brown, 1994; Brown and Bron, 1996); the governing factors are unknown but may relate in part to zonular traction and in part to the steady, but small, dehydration of the entire lens that begins in utero and continues postnatally (Bours and Fodisch, 1986). Growth of the lens after birth is considered in Chapter 12 (pp. 661-662).

Zonular development — the earliest fibres of the zonular apparatus are a continuation of the internal limiting membrane that thickens over the non-pigmented epithelium of the developing ciliary processes, beginning at about the tenth week of gestation (45 mm stage); later, zonular fibrils are synthesized by the ciliary epithelial cells, and the zonules increase in number, strength and coarseness, so that by the fifth month they have reached the lens and merge with both the anterior and posterior capsule; with formation of the zonulas the lens capsule is augmented by a zonular layer (Fig 17.67d) (p. 662).

Crystallin protein changes — the concentration of gamma-crystallin in the lens increases steadily throughout fetal life and reaches 23% of the total (crystallin) protein just before birth (Bessems et al., 1990); its synthesis ceases either just before birth (Thomson and Augusteyn, 1985) or at 5 or 6 years of age (Bours, 1980). The high proportion of gamma-crystallin may account, at least in part, for the greater transparency of the most central region of the lens (Bran and Brown, 1996) (p. 662).
content.blood_supply: During development the lens is vascularized by the hyaloid system: at 7 weeks of gestation, when the lumen of the lens vesicle is almost completely obliterated, capillaries of the hyaloid system provide the vascular supply to the lens (Fig 17.66e) (p. 660).
content.histology_summary: Structurally, the lens develops into three components: the capsule, the epithelium, and the lens cells or fibres (p. 661). Cellular polarity is established early: within the vesicle the apices of the cuboidal cells are directed toward the central cavity while the basal surface is outward and applied to the basal lamina that envelops the vesicle completely; with continued synthesis and secretion by the lens cells the basal lamina thickens and forms the lens capsule (Tripathi and Tripathi, 1983; 1984). Primary lens fibres attach firmly to the apical surface of the anterior lens epithelial cells through fascia adherens tight junctions, and the cell nuclei of the fibres, which also migrate anteriorly, eventually disintegrate and disappear; the posterior aspect of the lens therefore becomes devoid of epithelium (Tripathi and Tripathi, 1983). Note also the change in polarity of cells from anterior to posterior regions of the lens shown in Fig 17.67, and that attachment of the zonulas to the anterior, posterior and equatorial regions of the lens periphery becomes apparent as development proceeds, the capsule being augmented by a zonular layer (pp. 660-661).
content.clinical_importance: The Y sutures — an erect Y anteriorly and an inverted Y posteriorly, first seen at about the 35 mm stage (approximately 8.5 weeks of gestation) — persist through the entire thickness of the fetal nucleus and remain throughout life as a hallmark of lens development, providing a durable structural landmark within the adult lens. The high fetal proportion of gamma-crystallin (23% of total crystallin protein just before birth; Bessems et al., 1990) may account, at least in part, for the greater transparency of the most central region of the lens (Bran and Brown, 1996), and its synthesis ceases either just before birth (Thomson and Augusteyn, 1985) or at 5-6 years of age (Bours, 1980). The consumption of the posterior cells in forming the embryonic nucleus leaves the posterior aspect of the lens devoid of epithelium (Tripathi and Tripathi, 1983), and the near-spheroidal infantile shape with its equatorial predominance matures under factors that may include zonular traction and the small, steady dehydration of the lens beginning in utero (Bours and Fodisch, 1986); lens growth after birth is considered in Chapter 12 (pp. 661-662).
